title: VEX starter pack: thinking tools
entries: Confirmation bias

Seeking, noticing, and remembering evidence that supports what you already believe while ignoring what contradicts it. Counter: actively look for the strongest disconfirming evidence, and ask 'what would I expect to see if I were wrong?'
Sunk cost fallacy

Continuing something because of what you've already invested (money, time, effort) rather than what it will return from here. Past costs are gone either way. Ask: 'If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?'
Overconfidence
Being more certain than the evidence justifies. Most people's '90% sure' is right far less than 90% of the time. Counter: give ranges instead of points, and track your predictions.
Planning fallacy

Underestimating how long, costly, or hard a project will be, even when past projects ran over. Counter: use the outside view: how long did similar projects actually take? Then add a buffer of 25 to 50 percent.
Base rates

How often something happens in general, before your specific details. Most new restaurants close within a few years; most lottery tickets lose. Start with the base rate, then adjust for the specifics, usually less than you want to.
Survivorship bias

Drawing conclusions only from the winners you can see, while the failures are invisible. Dropout billionaires are visible; the many dropouts who struggled are not. Ask: 'Where are the ones who tried this and failed?'
Anchoring
Over-relying on the first number or idea you hear. Opening offers, list prices and first impressions anchor judgment. Counter: generate your own estimate before looking at anyone else's.
Availability heuristic
Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or dramatic events (plane crashes, viral stories) feel more common than they are. Check the actual numbers.
Dunning-Kruger effect

Beginners often overrate their skill because they don't yet know what they don't know; experts often underrate theirs. A quick sign: if something seems easy and you've never done it, you probably haven't seen the hard part yet.
Fundamental attribution error

Blaming other people's behavior on their character while blaming your own on circumstances. 'He's late because he's lazy; I'm late because of traffic.' Give others the same situational benefit of the doubt.
Loss aversion
Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains feel good, so people take bad risks to avoid losses and pass up good bets. Reframe decisions in terms of expected outcomes, not just avoiding loss.
Hindsight bias
After something happens, believing you 'knew it all along'. It makes outcomes seem more predictable than they were and blocks learning. Write predictions down before outcomes are known.
Mind reading
Assuming you know what someone else thinks or intends without evidence ('she thinks I'm stupid'). Counter: list other explanations, or simply ask them.
All-or-nothing thinking
Seeing things in extremes: total success or total failure, always or never. Reality is usually in between. Replace 'always' and 'never' with actual frequencies.
Catastrophizing
Jumping to the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely. Ask: what's the worst, best, and most likely outcome? What would I do if the worst happened?
Motivated reasoning
Reasoning toward the conclusion you want rather than following the evidence. Warning sign: you'd examine the opposite argument much more harshly. Apply the same standard of proof to both sides.
Straw man fallacy
Attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of what they actually said. The fix is the steelman: restate their view so well they'd agree, then respond.
Ad hominem
Attacking the person instead of the argument. A bad person can still make a correct point. Judge the claim on its evidence.
False dilemma
Presenting only two options when more exist ('either we do this or we fail'). Ask: what are the third, fourth, and fifth options, including doing nothing or doing a smaller version?
Slippery slope
Claiming one small step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome without showing why each step follows. Demand evidence for each link in the chain.
Correlation vs causation
Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. There may be a third cause, reverse causation, or coincidence. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of heat.
Appeal to authority
Accepting a claim because an authority said it, especially outside their expertise. Expertise matters, but ask what the evidence is and whether experts in that exact field agree.
Burden of proof
The person making a claim has to support it. 'You can't prove it's false' is not evidence that it's true.
Occam's razor
When several explanations fit the facts, prefer the one that needs the fewest extra assumptions. Not always right, but a good default.
Hanlon's razor
Don't assume malice when carelessness, ignorance, or misunderstanding explains it. Most slights are accidents.
First principles thinking
Break a problem down to its basic facts and rebuild from there instead of copying how it's usually done. Ask: what do we know is definitely true, and what is just convention?
Second-order thinking
Ask 'and then what?' Consider the consequences of the consequences. Quick wins often create long-term problems, and vice versa.
Inversion
Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you'd guarantee failure, then avoid those things. Also useful: argue the opposite of your conclusion.
Opportunity cost
The value of the best alternative you give up. Spending a year on project A costs you whatever else that year could have built. Always compare against the next-best use of time and money.
Expected value
Probability times payoff, summed across outcomes. A 10% chance at 1000 is worth about 100 on average. Good decisions can still have bad outcomes; judge the decision, not just the result.
Pre-mortem
Imagine it's a year from now and the plan failed. Write down why. This surfaces risks people are too optimistic to mention. Then fix the top three.
Steelmanning
Building the strongest possible version of an opposing view before arguing against it. If you can't state the other side's best argument, you don't understand the issue yet.
Circle of competence
Know the boundaries of what you actually understand. Inside it, trust your judgment more; outside it, slow down, ask experts, and be humble.
Pareto principle (80/20)
A small share of causes often produces most of the results: a few customers bring most revenue, a few habits drive most outcomes. Find the vital few and focus there.
Reversible vs irreversible decisions
Two-way-door decisions can be undone, so decide fast and learn. One-way-door decisions (quitting, big purchases, moving) deserve slow, careful thought.
Regret minimization
For big life choices, imagine yourself at 80 looking back. Which choice would you regret not making? Useful for cutting through short-term fear.
Decision matrix

List options as rows and criteria as columns, weight each criterion by importance, score each option 1 to 10, multiply and sum. It forces clarity and reveals when your gut disagrees with your stated priorities.
SMART goals
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. 'Get fit' becomes 'run 5 km without stopping by March 1, training three times a week.'
Habit loop
Cue, routine, reward. To build a habit, make the cue obvious, the action easy, and the reward immediate. To break one, remove the cue or add friction.
Implementation intentions
Plans in the form 'When X happens, I will do Y' are far more likely to be followed than vague intentions. Example: 'When I finish dinner, I will walk for 20 minutes.'
Feedback loops
Fast, honest feedback is how anyone improves. Shorten the loop: test small, measure, adjust. Long loops with no feedback are where people fool themselves for years.
Negotiation basics

Know your BATNA (best alternative if no deal), research the other side's interests not just positions, let them name a number first when you lack information, and trade things that are cheap for you but valuable to them.
Persuasion
People are moved by trust, emotion, and logic together. Listen first, find shared goals, use concrete stories and numbers, and make agreeing easy. Pushing harder usually triggers resistance.
Active listening
Reflect back what you heard, ask open questions, and don't plan your reply while they talk. Most arguments shrink once people feel understood.
Money basics

Spend less than you earn, keep an emergency fund of a few months of expenses, avoid high-interest debt, and invest consistently for the long term in diversified, low-cost funds. Get-rich-quick schemes mostly make the seller rich.
Startup reality

Most startups fail, usually from building something nobody wants or running out of money. Test demand cheaply before quitting a job: talk to customers, get pre-orders, run small experiments while you still have income.
Learning fast
Active recall (testing yourself) and spaced repetition beat rereading. Teach it to someone else (the Feynman technique) to find gaps. Practice the hard parts deliberately, with feedback.
Scientific thinking
Form a hypothesis, predict what you'd see if it's true, test it, and update. Be willing to say 'I was wrong'. Strong beliefs should require strong evidence.
Bayesian updating
Start with a prior belief, then shift it in proportion to how strong new evidence is. Weak evidence should move you a little; strong evidence a lot. Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence.
Spotting misinformation

Check the original source, the date, and who benefits. Look for whether other reliable outlets confirm it. Be extra skeptical of things that make you very angry or perfectly confirm what you already believe.
